Stan doesn't do Metropolis by default---it's using the NUTS
algorithm. The adapt_delta is not targeting "acceptance rate"
in the Metropolis sense, but the points along the Hamiltonian
simulation. See our manual or: http://www.jmlr.org/papers/v15/hoffman14a.html

But even basic HMC, which is a Metropolis algorithm, wants
an acceptance rate much higher than the one for Metropolis (and
keep in mind the Metropolis number was assming a normal posterior).
See: https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906

- Bob

parts: Hi Krishna,
Choice conjoint data set with 30 respondents and 20,000 iterations took 48 minutes to complete.

Why do you need 20,000 draws. Based on my experience this is complete overkill for these models. What's your effective sample size? Or... how many samples do you need for inference in your case? Do you use chains in parallel? What kind of machine are you using for computing? Renting a nice amazon machine for 2 hours isn't that expensive!

Most of the time I use 4 chains, 1,000 draws for warmup (check the trace plots!) and then 2,500 draws for each chain (== total post-warmup draws = 10,000). All R̂ R^s are < 1.0051.005. neffneff is > 2,000 for all relevant params... that's ok for me.

I'm now running the current successful code with another data set with 1,000 respondents and 20,000 iterations (alpha = 0.99 and stepsize = 0.1). It is still stuck on the 1 iteration of the sampling for the past 2.5 hours.

Again... why 20,000 draws? What about parallelization? And I don't think that you literally mean the first iteration, right?!? I never tried Choice Based Conjoint with more than 500 respondents (to expensive for me)... However, do you really need that many respondents in the analysis? What is the goal of the analysis? Are you interested in the estimated multivariate normal distribution of the utility parameters of do you need the individual level ββs? 

Question: Is this typical?

This is difficult to answer.. see above!

In another mail you asked:
Question: How do I extract individual level part-worths for each respondent from a stanfit object into a CSV file?

My hunch is you are indeed interested in the individual ββs. Given the example I posted earlier you need to do the following (and I think Ben already answered the question):

beta <- extract(res_stan, pars = "beta")[[1]]
str(beta) # array: n_draws x n_respondents x n_coef
means <- apply(beta, 2:3, mean)
str(means) # matrix: n_respondents x n_coef
write.csv(means, file = "means.csv")

I urge you not to use only the posterior means in the next steps of your analysis because one nice feature of the HB estimation is that you get the full posterior distribution. I guess you're not only going show the posterior means in a big table in your paper but you are running (also) some sort of non-linear transformations (e.g., market simulation, What'if simulation, profit maximization, ...). The uncertainty in your individual level estimates will be quite large because of the low number of obs. for each respondet. Hence plugging in your posterior means in your non-linear transformations might actually be misleading...

One last point regarding speed: maybe for you it is worth considering classical methods (=> maximum simulated likelihood). mlogit is nice and very fast in R, because you integrate the heterogeneity out of your likelihood. In a second step you can use importance sampling to derive the conditional estimates of each respondent given his/her choices and the estimated heterogeneity distribution (see Kenneth Trains book chapter 11 here. AFAIK this is even implemented in gmnl (see Sarrias / Daziano (2015)). Don't get me wrong... I'm not saying this is the best way but it will do the job in your case (because you only want a point estimates), it is easy to implement and it is quite fast (even with many respondents). Once you have estimated the (“representative”) heterogeneity distribution this procedure scales linearly with the number of respondents.

Hope this helps!

Best,
Daniel 

PS: whoever is interested in discrete choice models + R ... contact me via “daniel.guhl at hu-berlin.de“
